note.explanation: The cell cycle is an ordered series of events in which a eukaryotic cell grows, copies its DNA, and divides into two daughter cells. Interphase includes G1, S, and G2. In G0, some cells stop dividing to carry out special functions.
examples: In S phase, the DNA is copied, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Neurons can remain in G0 for an indefinite period, while epithelial cells continue to divide.
note.checkAnswer: S phase; the DNA is replicated, and the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
note.simple: A cell grows, copies its DNA, prepares, and then divides. Some cells pause dividing in G0.
note.checkQuestion: In which phase is the DNA of each chromosome replicated?
note.title: The Cell Cycle: Growth, DNA Copying and Division
steps: After M phase, the cell enters G1 and grows.
In S phase, the cell copies its DNA.
In G2 phase, the cell grows further and prepares for division.
In M phase, the cell divides into two daughter cells.
Some cells may leave the cycle and enter G0.
note.answer: The cell cycle is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.

mcqs.stem: A cell has copied the DNA of each chromosome, but the total number of chromosomes has not changed. Which phase has just occurred?
rationales: G1 is mainly a growth and preparation phase before DNA replication.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, while the chromosome number remains the same.
G2 follows DNA replication and includes further growth and preparation for division.
M phase is the division phase, not the phase in which DNA is copied.

mcqs.stem: During which phase does a cell make proteins and organelles and grow in size?
rationales: G1 is the growth phase in which the cell makes proteins and organelles.
S phase is primarily for DNA replication.
G2 includes further growth and production of proteins needed for cell division.
G0 is a phase in which some cells stop dividing to perform specialized functions.

options: The cell prepares for division and goes through growth and DNA replication.

rationales: Interphase includes growth, preparation, and DNA replication before division.
Some cells stop dividing in G0, but this does not describe interphase.
Sister chromatids separate during cell division, not interphase.
DNA is replicated in S phase, which is part of interphase, but this option does not describe all of interphase.

mcqs.stem: Which option gives the usual order of the main cell-cycle phases?
rationales: The phases proceed through G1, S, G2, and then M.
S occurs after G1, and M occurs after G2, so this order is incorrect.
G2 follows S, and M follows G2, so this order is incorrect.
G1 begins after M, so this sequence does not give the usual order.

mcqs.stem: Which event is most closely associated with G0 phase?
rationales: Growth and preparation for DNA replication are associated with G1.
DNA replication occurs in S phase.
Checking for DNA damage and preparing for mitosis are associated with G2.
In G0, some cells leave the cycle and stop dividing, often to perform specialized functions.

options: It lasts for about 90% of the total time of the cell cycle.
It is the phase in which the cell divides into two daughter cells.

rationales: Interphase lasts for about 90% of the total time of the cell cycle.
The division into daughter cells occurs in the M phase.

explain.title: What is the cell cycle?
explain.body: The textbook defines it as: “It is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.” The cell cycle has two main phases: interphase and the mitosis phase.

explain.title: Interphase: most of the cell cycle
explain.body: Interphase lasts for about 90% of the total time of the cell cycle. The cell performs its life functions and prepares for the next division. It consists of G1, S, and G2 phases.

explain.title: G1 and S phases
explain.body: G1 is also called the growth phase: the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and makes enzymes needed in S phase. In S phase, the DNA of each chromosome is copied. Each chromosome then consists of two sister chromatids, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.

explain.title: G2, M, and G0 phases
explain.body: In G2, the cell grows further, makes proteins for division, checks for DNA damage, and prepares for mitosis. After interphase, M phase divides the cell into two daughter cells. Some cells enter G0 and stop dividing while carrying out specialized functions; neurons may remain there indefinitely, while epithelial cells continue to divide.

mistakes: Do not say that the chromosome number doubles in S phase; the DNA is copied, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Do not confuse G1 and G2: G1 is the first growth phase, while G2 follows DNA replication and includes preparation for division.
Do not say that every cell enters G0; the textbook notes that some cells, such as epithelial cells, continue to divide without entering G0.
Do not describe interphase as a resting phase; the cell performs life functions, grows, copies DNA, and prepares for division.
